profiles.name: National Library of Medicine
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: National Library of Medicine
originalProfile.summary: The National Library of Medicine (NLM) is a federal library founded in 1836, part of the National Institutes of Health under the Department of Health and Human Services, based in Bethesda, Maryland. It describes itself as the world's largest biomedical library and runs PubMed/MEDLINE, MedlinePlus, and ClinicalTrials.gov alongside a History of Medicine division that publishes online exhibitions such as Changing the Face of Medicine and Opening Doors. The NIH parent site separately publishes NIH Research Matters, a weekly research-highlights column edited by NIH's Office of Communications and Public Liaison and reviewed by NIH staff scientists.
originalProfile.relevance: BlackStory cites NLM exhibition pages for biographies of Black physicians and surgeons, including Alexa Canady and Jane Cooke Wright, and for institution histories such as Provident Hospital in Chicago and Mercy-Douglass Hospital. It cites the nih.gov Research Matters column for reporting on federally funded research with African American historical subject matter, such as ancestry findings from the Catoctin Furnace burial site, and cites pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov as a journal-article index for institutions like Good Samaritan Hospital in Selma.
limitations: The exhibition biography pages are curatorial summaries written for a general audience, not primary archival documents, and do not always carry footnoted sourcing on the page itself.
PubMed entries index a journal article's metadata and abstract; the article's own content sits behind the publisher, not on nih.gov.
NIH Research Matters covers a study's findings as reported by NIH staff, not the underlying peer-reviewed paper itself.

originalProfile.name: National Register of Historic Places / NPGallery Digital Asset Search (National Park Service)
originalProfile.summary: NPGallery is the National Park Service's digital asset search platform for the National Register of Historic Places and National Historic Landmarks programs. It is operated by NPS, a division of the U.S. Department of the Interior, and holds the official nomination forms, reference numbers, and designation records for properties the federal government has recognized as historically significant. Records are searchable by resource name, location, and reference number.
originalProfile.relevance: BlackStory cites this host overwhelmingly for place records, almost all carrying the predicate designated_national_historic_landmark or a 'listed on [register]' statement drawn from official NRHP nomination data, plus a handful of person, institution, organization and school records.
limitations: The site is a search/document-retrieval interface, not an interpretive narrative source; nomination forms vary widely in depth and era of scholarship
Older nomination forms (pre-1990s) can reflect the historical framing and omissions typical of their period
PDF nomination forms are sometimes scanned/OCR'd and can have transcription artifacts

profiles.name: Wikipedia (English)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Wikipedia (English)
originalProfile.summary: Wikipedia is the free, crowd-edited online encyclopedia operated by the Wikimedia Foundation. Any registered or anonymous user can create or edit an article; quality control comes from community review, citation requirements, and administrator oversight rather than a fixed editorial staff. Coverage depth and sourcing rigor vary widely by article.
originalProfile.relevance: Wikipedia is cited broadly as a general-purpose bridge and summary source spread across nearly every entity kind in the catalog: place, person, organization, institution, event, school, case, law, publication, and movement records.
limitations: Anyone can edit an article; content can be incomplete, outdated, or vandalized between reviews
Sourcing quality varies by article and editor community
Per project rule, must never be the sole basis for a 'first'/'only'/superlative claim (the William F. Penn/Yale Medicine incident is the cautionary case on file)
Should be treated as a lead to primary/institutional sources, not as corroboration itself

profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: National Park Service (nps.gov)
originalProfile.summary: The National Park Service is the U.S. Department of the Interior agency established in 1916 to preserve and interpret national parks, monuments, and historic sites. nps.gov publishes park and site pages, 'people' and 'places' interpretive content, and heritage-program materials, produced by NPS staff historians and interpreters with input from partner organizations and volunteers.
originalProfile.relevance: NPS is cited both for park/site documentation and for biographical/interpretive content about people connected to those sites, concentrated on place records (mostly 'documented_site' or 'commemorates') and person records, with smaller counts for event, organization, school, law, movement, institution, and invention.
limitations: Interpretive/park pages are written for a visitor audience and vary in citation depth
Coverage reflects which sites fall under NPS management or partnership programs, not comprehensive national coverage
Content is updated unevenly across thousands of park unit pages

originalProfile.name: National Inventors Hall of Fame (invent.org)
originalProfile.summary: The National Inventors Hall of Fame is a nonprofit organization that inducts and documents inventors judged to have made a lasting contribution to innovation, through an annual nomination and induction process. invent.org publishes inductee profiles, blog content, and an inductee search/list.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as a source specifically for inventor biography and invention attribution ('source states', 'inspired'), split between invention and person records.
limitations: Selection criteria for induction are not fully documented on the pages reviewed
Inductee profiles are promotional/biographical in tone, produced with the inductee's cooperation, not independent investigative research

originalProfile.name: Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc.
originalProfile.summary: This is the official website of Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc., the first intercollegiate Greek-letter fraternity founded for African American men, established December 4, 1906 at Cornell University by seven founders known as "the Jewels." The site's own history section documents the founders and the fraternity's civil rights history in its own words.
originalProfile.relevance: BlackStory cites apa1906.net for person entities (individual founders, e.g. Charles Henry Chapman, George Biddle Kelley) and the organization entity itself, all citing the same /our-history/ page for founding facts and founder identification.
limitations: As the subject organization's own site, it is not an independent source about itself; useful for self-reported founding facts but not for external corroboration of the same claims.
Biographical detail on individual founders beyond their role in the founding is thin on this page.

originalProfile.name: BlackPast.org
originalProfile.summary: BlackPast.org is a nonprofit online reference founded in January 2004 by Quintard Taylor, the Scott and Dorothy Bullitt Professor of American History at the University of Washington. It began as a research aid featuring short entries on people, places, and events in African American and global Black history and has grown into one of the largest dedicated Black-history reference resources online.
originalProfile.relevance: Used broadly as a biographical and topical reference across nearly every entity kind, dominated by person records under 'source states' or biographical predicates (e.g., 'chaired'), plus place, organization, event, movement, case, law, institution, and publication records.
limitations: A single-organization reference project, not a peer-reviewed academic journal; entry depth and citation rigor vary by contributor
As a reputable secondary source it still needs an independent institutional lineage before anchoring a superlative claim

profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: The Historical Marker Database (HMdb.org)
originalProfile.summary: HMdb.org is a volunteer-run, crowd-submitted database transcribing the text of physical historical markers across the U.S. and beyond. Anyone can submit a new marker page or edit an existing one; submissions are queued and reviewed by one of dozens of volunteer editors (drawn from thousands of contributing correspondents over 20+ years) before publication.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as a source for on-the-ground historical-marker text tied to specific sites, almost entirely place records under the predicate documented_site, with smaller counts for person, event, organization, school, and institution records.
limitations: Crowd-submitted: markers are transcribed and photographed by volunteers, not centrally researched by an institution
Editorial review exists (volunteer editors screen submissions) but is not equivalent to institutional/archival review
Content quality is the marker text itself, which can repeat errors or dated framing from the original marker's installation era

originalProfile.name: Virginia Department of Historic Resources (DHR)
originalProfile.summary: Virginia DHR is the Commonwealth's State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO), a state agency within the Natural and Historic Resources Secretariat. It administers the Virginia Landmarks Register (over 3,300 individual resources and 600+ historic districts), the state's Historic Highway Marker program (2,500+ markers), and Virginia's National Register of Historic Places nominations, compiled through professional-staff research and quarterly review by the Board of Historic Resources and State Review Board.
originalProfile.relevance: Used for Virginia-specific historic designation and marker records, almost entirely place records with smaller organization and person counts.
limitations: Coverage limited to Virginia
Older marker text (some markers date to the mid-20th century) can reflect the historiographical framing of its installation era even when the underlying agency is current

originalProfile.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica (britannica.com)
originalProfile.summary: Encyclopaedia Britannica is a commercial reference publisher dating to 1768 in Scotland, now operated online by Encyclopaedia Britannica, Inc. Entries are written and updated by subject-area editorial staff and outside contributing specialists, then reviewed by an editorial team and passed through a fact-checking process before publication.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as a general biographical reference source, overwhelmingly for person records (e.g. 'pulitzer_prizes', 'hall_of_fame_induction_year' predicates) with a few event, case, and organization records.
limitations: A commercial general encyclopedia, not a specialist Black-history institution
classifySourceForConfidence currently has no dedicated classification for it (falls to 'unknown'), so it is treated the same as an unclassified host despite its editorial process
Under the project's rule, 'unknown'/commercial encyclopedic sources should not anchor a superlative alone

originalProfile.name: Library of Congress (loc.gov, guides.loc.gov, blogs.loc.gov)
originalProfile.summary: The Library of Congress is the research library of the U.S. Congress and the de facto national library, holding digitized primary-source collections (manuscripts, photographs, newspapers), curated research guides, and staff-written blog posts that draw on those collections.
originalProfile.relevance: Used both for biographical documentation ('documented_by', 'source states') and as the source for historic publication entries, split fairly evenly between person and place records, plus publication records (notably historic Black newspapers), and smaller organization, event, law, movement, and invention counts.
limitations: Blog posts (blogs.loc.gov) are staff secondary narration, one step removed from the primary digitized record
Digitized-collection coverage is uneven across eras and subject areas

Repo note on file: this project already knows the William F. Penn/Yale Medicine superlative error traced through a civil-rights-leaders LOC-linked entity, underscoring that even LOC-hosted pages can carry an unverified secondary claim if the underlying assertion originates elsewhere

profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute (LII)
originalProfile.summary: LII is a non-profit public service of Cornell Law School, founded in 1992 by Peter Martin and Tom Bruce, that provides free access to U.S. Code, Supreme Court opinions (all decisions since 1990 plus 600+ historic pre-1992 cases), federal regulations and rules, and Wex, a legal encyclopedia edited by vetted legal experts and Cornell Law students.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as BlackStory's primary source for case-law text and holdings, almost entirely case records under the predicate 'source states' with a handful of law records.
limitations: Repo-documented issue: LII's case transcriptions carry known OCR corruption; this project's own rule directs quoting SCOTUS opinions from tile.loc.gov US Reports PDFs instead of LII transcriptions for direct quotation
A university-hosted convenience republication, not the court's own official reporter

originalProfile.name: Google Patents (mirroring USPTO records)
originalProfile.summary: Google Patents is Google's search and full-text interface over patent data, built by crawling and packaging USPTO (and other patent offices') public data; Google formerly mirrored USPTO PAIR bulk data directly, though the USPTO now serves current data itself via its Bulk Data Storage System. For an individual patent document, the text displayed is the same official specification issued by the Patent Office.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as the primary source for patent-grant facts (patent number, filing/issue date, inventor of record) for Black inventors profiled in BlackStory, mostly on invention records under the predicate 'source states' with a handful of person records.
limitations: Per this project's binding fitness rule: a patent is authoritative for who filed what and when, and unfit as evidence of the filer's race, of firstness, or of adoption/impact
Only resolvable individual patent-document pages get government_record treatment; a search or listing page on the same host does not
Patent text reflects legal-filing language, not biographical or historical narrative

originalProfile.name: History.com (A+E Global Media)
originalProfile.summary: History.com is the companion website of the HISTORY cable channel, published by A+E Global Media, a joint venture between Hearst Communications and Disney Entertainment Television (part of The Walt Disney Company). It is a commercial media property; some programming involves professional historians, but the site itself is not an academic or archival institution.
originalProfile.relevance: Used as a general popular-history reference, including for date-specific predicates like became_first_woman_inducted_date and sworn_in_on, mostly on person records with smaller movement, event, place, and organization counts.
limitations: Commercial media property, not an archive or academic publisher
The channel/site has drawn documented criticism from scholars over factual rigor in some of its programming
classifySourceForConfidence has no dedicated classification for it, so it is currently treated the same as any unclassified host

originalProfile.name: Office of the Historian, U.S. House of Representatives (history.house.gov)
originalProfile.summary: The Office of the Historian, working with the Clerk of the House's Office of Art and Archives, is the legislative-branch office responsible for preserving, collecting, and interpreting the history of the U.S. House of Representatives, including biographical profiles of every member since 1789, oral histories, and thematic histories (e.g., Black Americans in Congress).
originalProfile.relevance: Used specifically for congressional-service biographical facts and legislative history, mostly person records (predicates like served_as, first_to, elected_on) plus law, invention, and place records.
limitations: Scope limited to matters touching the House of Representatives
Biographical profiles are official-record summaries, not full independent biographies

originalProfile.name: National Center for Education Statistics (nces.ed.gov)
originalProfile.summary: NCES is the primary statistical agency of the U.S. Department of Education, located within the Institute of Education Sciences, with a Congressional mandate to collect, analyze, and report comprehensive U.S. education statistics under standards of timeliness, credibility, objectivity, and respondent confidentiality.
originalProfile.relevance: Used specifically as the source for HBCU (Historically Black College/University) institutional records in BlackStory, entirely under the predicate 'source states' on place records.
limitations: The about page reviewed did not include HBCU-specific data documentation; general NCES data-quality standards were confirmed, not the specific dataset behind these claims
Federal statistical data reflects institution self-reporting to NCES surveys, subject to standard survey-response limitations

profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Smithsonian Magazine
originalProfile.summary: Smithsonian magazine is published by the Smithsonian Institution but is editorially independent of it. Founded in 1970 by former Life editor Edward K. Thompson at the request of Smithsonian Secretary S. Dillon Ripley, it puts "a Smithsonian lens on the world" (science, history, art, popular culture and innovation)for a general readership. It is a staffed magazine with reporters and editors, not a primary archive or museum record.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited across person biography, event narrative (e.g. the Elaine Massacre), and invention-history claims, split among person, event, and invention records. Sample predicates: source_states, broke_color_line_at, resulted_in, became.
limitations: Magazine journalism, not a primary or archival record: it synthesizes and cites other sources rather than being the underlying document.
Not classified as tier1/tier2 by the repo's confidence code despite institutional Smithsonian ties, because the domain differs from si.edu and carries no source-register entry.
General-audience feature writing can compress or simplify complex historical disputes.

profiles.name: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture
originalProfile.summary: NMAAHC is the Smithsonian Institution's museum devoted exclusively to African American life, history and culture, established by Act of Congress in 2003 and opened September 24, 2016 as the Smithsonian's 19th museum. It holds more than 45,000 artifacts and is led by a professional curatorial staff; founding director Lonnie G. Bunch III shaped its mission to "capture and share the unvarnished truth" of African American history.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited broadly for person biography and achievement claims, mostly on person records, plus institution, event, place, and publication records. Sample predicates: became, built, organized, honored_with.
limitations: A federally chartered museum, not a court or vital-records office: authoritative for its own exhibits/collections and curatorial scholarship, not a substitute for a primary legal or genealogical record.
Web content (object labels, digital stories) is written for public audiences and may summarize rather than fully cite underlying primary sources.

profiles.name: Encyclopedia Virginia
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Encyclopedia Virginia
originalProfile.summary: Encyclopedia Virginia is a project of Virginia Humanities in partnership with the Library of Virginia, and since 2012 has served as the digital publisher of the Library of Virginia's Dictionary of Virginia Biography. Entries are written by scholars and put through developmental editing, fact-checking, section-editor review and separate copy-editing before publication, with especially complex or controversial entries getting multiple scholar reviews.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for Virginia case holdings, person life-events, and event narrative, plus a law entity, across case, event, law, person, place, and publication kinds. Sample predicates: held (case), site_of, elected_on, organized.
limitations: Editorially reviewed but not traditional academic peer review by the site's own description: it names this a distinct, lighter-weight process.
State-scoped: authoritative for Virginia subjects, not a general national reference.
No national-library authority-control record (per tier1-sources.ts commentary), which is why it sits on the curated list rather than in source-register.json.

profiles.name: Lemelson-MIT Program
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Lemelson-MIT Program
originalProfile.summary: The Lemelson-MIT Program is an invention-education initiative established at MIT in 1994 and administered by MIT's School of Engineering, funded primarily by the Lemelson Foundation. It produces invention-education curricula, an inventor archive and handbook, case studies and research reports rather than functioning as a museum or a formal library archive.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for invention attribution and inventor-biography claims, split between invention and person kinds, mostly on a 'source_states' predicate: e.g. what a given inventor patented or built.
limitations: An education/outreach program, not a patent office or museum registrar: its inventor profiles are secondary retellings, useful as a lead into the underlying patent or archival record.
Focused on inventors and invention history specifically; not a general biographical source.

profiles.name: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
originalProfile.summary: NASA is the U.S. federal agency for civil aeronautics and space exploration, founded in 1958 and operating across 20 centers and facilities. nasa.gov publishes astronaut biographies, an 'Astronaut Fact Book,' mission histories and news content produced by internal page editors and public-affairs staff, alongside blogs, videos and podcasts.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for astronaut and NASA-employee career and mission-milestone claims, overwhelmingly on person records plus an invention entity. Sample predicates: worked_at, became, flew, piloted.
limitations: Public-affairs content, not a personnel archive; useful for career/mission facts NASA itself records, less so for facts outside its own operations.
Some historical astronaut pages are periodically updated/rewritten, so wording and emphasis can shift over time.

profiles.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Encyclopedia of Alabama
originalProfile.summary: The Encyclopedia of Alabama's original content is copyrighted by the Alabama Humanities Alliance; its editorial office is administered by Auburn University's Office of University Outreach with University Libraries. Entries are written by scholars and subject specialists "from academic institutions to scientists in the field" and cover Alabama's history, culture, geography and natural environment; it won the Alabama Historical Association's inaugural Digital History Award (2016) and Library Journal's 'Best of Free Reference.'
originalProfile.relevance: Cited across person biography, event narrative, invention, organization, and place claims for Alabama subjects, with person records the largest share. Sample predicates: built, source_states, delivered.
limitations: The site describes editorial oversight for trustworthiness but does not detail a formal peer-review procedure the way Encyclopedia Virginia does.
State-scoped to Alabama subjects.
Corrections require 'verifiable, reliable sources' but the site says it won't revise entries over differing interpretation alone: a caveat on contested claims.

profiles.name: Lowcountry Digital History Initiative (College of Charleston Libraries)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Lowcountry Digital History Initiative (College of Charleston Libraries)
originalProfile.summary: LDHI is a digital public-history platform based at the College of Charleston, a public South Carolina university, that publishes free online exhibitions on South Carolina Lowcountry history, prioritizing narratives underrepresented in mainstream historical discourse. It's built through a collaborative model of academic scholars, public historians, community members, librarians and archivists, with College of Charleston graduate students serving as assistant curators on individual exhibits.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for South Carolina Lowcountry person-narrative claims, overwhelmingly on person records plus a law entity. Sample predicates: killed, convicted_after, part_of: several tied to the 2015 Emanuel AME Church shooting and its aftermath.
limitations: Individual exhibits are curated by graduate-student assistant curators under faculty supervision, so depth and sourcing rigor can vary exhibit to exhibit.
Regionally scoped to the South Carolina Lowcountry.

profiles.name: Oklahoma Historical Society
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Oklahoma Historical Society
originalProfile.summary: The Oklahoma Historical Society is, by its own description, both a state government agency and a private membership organization, founded May 27, 1893 by the Territorial Press Association and governed by a 25-member Board of Directors. It collects, preserves and shares Oklahoma history and culture through a statewide network of museums, historic homes, research centers and military sites, plus publications and a historical-marker program.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for Oklahoma place designation/listing and case-history claims, mostly place records with a smaller count of case records. Sample predicates: source_states, decided_on, held, listed_on_national_register.
limitations: Not on the .gov TLD, so the repo's confidence code cannot distinguish it from a commercial or unknown host even though it functions as a state agency: the code result (tier3) is more conservative than the organization's actual institutional status.
Dual government/membership-organization structure means not every page on the site is an official state-agency determination.

profiles.name: National Trust for Historic Preservation
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: National Trust for Historic Preservation
originalProfile.summary: The National Trust for Historic Preservation is a private 501(c)(3) nonprofit, operating independently for more than 75 years, that leads preservation advocacy for historic sites across the U.S. Its website (savingplaces.org) publishes grant and program information, stories from its Preservation Magazine, guidance on historic sites open to visit, and advocacy/press content; it also operates affiliated entities including Main Street America and the National Trust Community Investment Corporation.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for place/building history and civil-rights-site significance claims, plus person residence claims, across person, place, and school records. Sample predicates: source_states, civil_rights_role, building_history, resided_at_years.
limitations: An advocacy nonprofit, not the federal listing authority (the National Park Service administers the National Register itself); its site content discusses significance but isn't the NRHP nomination document.
Magazine-style storytelling for a general and donor-facing audience.

profiles.name: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute (Stanford University)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute (Stanford University)
originalProfile.summary: The King Institute is an academic research center at Stanford University, home to the Martin Luther King, Jr. Papers Project since Coretta Scott King asked Stanford historian Clayborne Carson in 1985 to edit King's papers; the Institute proper was established in 2005. It publishes the multi-volume Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr., a King Encyclopedia of more than 280 articles on civil-rights figures, events and organizations, and a day-to-day King chronology, all built on the Papers Project's original archival research.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for civil-rights movement and event-narrative claims, across event, movement, organization, person, and place records. Sample predicates: source_states, occurred_in, closed_in, organized_by: Albany Movement, Birmingham Campaign, March on Washington.
limitations: Deep on King and the movements/institutions around him; thinner for civil-rights subjects outside that orbit.
The Institute does not hold reproduction rights to King's own works: a licensing caveat, not a factual-accuracy one.

profiles.name: United States Senate (Senate Historical Office)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: United States Senate (Senate Historical Office)
originalProfile.summary: senate.gov is the official website of the U.S. Senate. Its historical content (origins and development of the Senate, historical highlights from 1787 to present, biographical records of senators, and Senate procedures and traditions)is produced by the Senate Historical Office, which the site credits by name on its history pages and which takes public questions from a named Senate historian.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for Black U.S. senators' election and swearing-in dates and for law-entity claims, split between person records (elected_on/sworn_in_on predicates) and law records.
limitations: Authoritative for the Senate's own institutional history and membership record, not a general source for legislative history outside the Senate's own actions.
Historical-highlight pages are written for public education and may summarize rather than reproduce full documentary detail.

profiles.name: Rosenwald Fund Collection, Fisk University (John Hope and Aurelia E. Franklin Library)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: Rosenwald Fund Collection, Fisk University (John Hope and Aurelia E. Franklin Library)
originalProfile.summary: The Rosenwald Fund Collection is Fisk University's digitized archive of the Julius Rosenwald Fund's records (585 archival boxes and an estimated 674,000 items)documenting Rosenwald's philanthropy and its impact on Black education, maintained by Fisk's Franklin Library and expanded through the Mellon Foundation-funded 'Forging Future Pathways' digitization project. The searchable school-card database draws on the Fund's original school cards, financial records, applications and photographs for the roughly 5,000 Rosenwald schools built across 15 Southern states.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited exclusively for Rosenwald-school site documentation and operating-years claims, entirely on school records. Sample predicates: documented_site, active_years.
limitations: The card-file data reflects the Fund's own administrative records; a school's actual construction/closure dates can occasionally diverge from what the card recorded.
The full 674,000-item archive is still being digitized in phases, so coverage of the broader Rosenwald Fund collection beyond the school cards is incomplete.

profiles.name: NPR (National Public Radio)
profiles.reason: Existing descriptive claims are not recertified by a collection page. Use document-relative evidence review; old profile dates are historical.

originalProfile.name: NPR (National Public Radio)
originalProfile.summary: NPR is an independent, nonprofit public-media organization founded in 1970 that produces and distributes news and cultural programming to a network of nearly 250 member stations, funded through a mix of listener support, sponsorship and government support. Its editorial operations are governed by a published Ethics Handbook and overseen by an independent Public Editor; NPR states it does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
originalProfile.relevance: Cited for person career and civil-rights event-narrative claims, overwhelmingly on person records. Sample predicates: sworn_in_on, beaten_on, chart_record, attacked_at: several tied to civil-rights-movement violence.
limitations: Not classified tier1/tier2 by the repo's confidence code: 'npr' contains none of the NEWS_HOST_HINTS substrings ('news','times','post','tribune','gazette','herald') the code checks for, so it falls to 'unknown' despite being a substantial news organization.

originalProfile.name: Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum

originalProfile.summary: The Smithsonian Institution was founded in 1846 under James Smithson's bequest and describes itself as the world's largest museum, education, and research complex, encompassing numerous museums and the National Zoo, research centers, cultural centers, education centers, and collections. originalProfile.relevance: BlackStory cites si.edu pages for museum object records with catalog metadata and captions, such as a painting of Bethlehem Baptist Church held by the Anacostia Community Museum, for biographical features on inventors and pioneers like Mary Beatrice Kenner and Bessie Coleman, for a women's history blog post, for an SOVA finding aid describing the United Negro College Fund's records, and for the Smithsonian's affiliate-museum directory listing the African American Museum in Philadelphia.
limitations: si.edu spans many separately curated units and content types, from formal museum object catalogs to blog posts and podcast transcripts, with uneven citation practices between them.
Narrative features like Sidedoor and 'collections snapshot' pages are written for a general audience and summarize history rather than reproducing primary documents.
The affiliate directory describes an institutional partnership with the Smithsonian, not the affiliate's own history, and should not be read as a primary source for the affiliate itself.
